title: Bedtime prayers
hookLine: Now I lay me down to sleep: children's prayers carried for life

lines: THE HALLWAY LIGHT, THE DOOR AJAR.
NOW I LAY ME DOWN TO SLEEP.
YEARS LATER, THE WORDS COME BACK.
cards: The bedroom light is off. Only the hallway lamp is on, and the door is open a crack. A small voice comes from under a blanket: "Now I lay me down to sleep, I pray the Lord my soul to keep."
A parent sits on the edge of the bed and says it along. Years go by. The child grows up and stops saying it.
Then one night, in a strange bed, a hospital, a hotel, the night before something hard, the words come back on their own.

teach.h: NOW I LAY ME DOWN TO SLEEP.
teach.b: In its old form, the children's prayer goes: "Now I lay me down to sleep, I pray the Lord my soul to keep; If I should die before I wake, I pray the Lord my soul to take."

It isn't a Bible verse, and its third line can startle a modern parent. Some families keep it; some swap in a gentler line. Before letting go of the day, a child hands themselves over to God's keeping.

teach.h: I LAID ME DOWN AND SLEPT; I AWAKED.
teach.b: One psalm's heading sets it when David fled from Absalom, his own son, and it says: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me." Enemies all around, and he sleeps.
Another psalm ends: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." Lying down becomes an act of trust. Then, the one who doesn't sleep.

teach.h: HE SHALL NEITHER SLUMBER NOR SLEEP.
teach.b: Psalm one hundred twenty-one: "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep." You can close your eyes because someone else is keeping watch. Last, the grown-up version.
The old English prayer book gives the church an evening prayer: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night."

The child's request, in longer words. Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants each have their own night prayers, alone or together. For some, the children's prayer is still the one that comes first in the dark.

how: Some Christian parents teach children a short prayer to say at bedtime, such as "Now I lay me down to sleep"; Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants also have longer evening and night prayers, said at home or in church.

games.q: you're David, running from your own son's army. enemies are all around, and night is falling. what do you do?
o: stay awake on guard all night.
games.why: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me." sleep, in the psalm, is an act of trust.

practice: Lie down if it's night, or sit back and let your shoulders drop as if it were, and let the day go one piece at a time: the conversations, the tasks, the thing you didn't finish.

If you pray, you can say the children's prayer or the psalm on the screen slowly, the way you'd hand something to someone you trust; if you don't, notice what it would feel like to set the whole day down and let someone else keep watch.

wordCard.voice: Bedtime prayers. The words said before sleep, handing the night over to God's keeping, sometimes learned as a child and kept for life.
